Question 10(c) [6 marks]: Explain the importance of myths and legends relating to the Minoans during this period.

MARKING CRITERIA (out of 6):
6 marks: Provides a detailed and informed explanation of features relevant to the question | Communicates effectively using appropriate terms and concepts
4–5 marks: Provides an informed explanation of features relevant to the question | Communicates using appropriate terms and concepts
2–3 marks: Provides some information about features relevant to the question | May use some appropriate terms and/or concepts
1 marks: Makes a general statement(s) relevant to the question

SAMPLE ANSWER (official):
Myths and legends relating to the Minoans tell us much about their society. The myth of the Minotaur tells of King Minos, a legendary ruler of Crete. He ruled over the Aegean people and established a thalassocracy. King Minos accepted tribute from his subjects, including Athens, and took young men and women every year to feed the Minotaur, a mythical half-man and half-bull monster which occupied the labyrinth under the palace at Knossos. This myth ties to the Minoan civilisation through the frequency of bull motifs, the use of Minos as a possible title for kings, the idea of the Minoan thalassocracy, and the maze of magazines under the Palace at Knossos which could be thought to represent a labyrinth. Some historians link the Minotaur with Baal-Moloch, a Canaanite god associated with child sacrifice. The myth of Daedalus and Icarus represents the importance of engineering and technology. Daedalus, whose name translates to ‘genius’, was credited with inventing carpentry as well as the saw, axe, plumbline, drill and glue.
The Minoans were advanced in many forms of engineering, such as ashlar masonry, running water and toilets, roads and earthquake-proof housing.
